[0] Privacy search engine company DuckDuckGo has released a new survey revealing how much personal information users share with AI chatbots, and how little many people actually understand about where these conversations go. Here are the details.

[1] The survey shows that AI users share more information than they realise

[2] DuckDuckGo's survey, released today, highlights a number of privacy concerns related to AI chatbot use, including the finding that nearly one-third of users have told an AI things they would not say to friends, family, colleagues, or medical professionals. Among those who identify as AI enthusiasts, this proportion rises even further to 56%.

[3] DuckDuckGo said:

[4] The company pointed out that, among nearly 2,000 American adult respondents, 53% did not know or were unsure whether most chatbots default to using conversations to train models, while only 25% knew that AI conversations can be subpoenaed by law enforcement.

[5] The survey results also revealed a significant behavioural gap between parents and non-parents, with parents or guardians of young children confiding in AI at almost twice the rate of non-parents. DuckDuckGo noted that "among AI-using parents, 43% have told an AI something they have never shared with anyone," while "among AI users without children at home, this proportion drops to 25%."

[6] DuckDuckGo believes that AI companies have consistently encouraged users to treat chatbots as a confidant—whether in advertising or in public appearances—but the reality is that these conversations may not be as private as users have been led to believe.

[7] As for trust, the survey found that people have slightly more confidence in large AI companies to protect their data than in the US government. However, scepticism runs high towards both: 39% of respondents said they have no trust at all in large AI companies, while 48% said the same about the government.

[8] DuckDuckGo concluded by noting that users still have an opportunity to change the way they treat AI privacy, particularly since our habits around chatbot use are still relatively new:

[9] "When we talk about online privacy with search engines and browsers, a lot of people think 'it's too late, my data is already out there.' But the truth is, the most valuable information you share with big tech is your next question, not the ones you asked days, months, or years ago. So it's never too late to switch to more privacy-respecting online services."

[10] The company also reminded users that they can take proactive steps to protect their privacy when using AI chatbots, including choosing services with clearer and more transparent data handling policies.
